shanti.1: Om. That (the unseen Brahman) is whole; this (the seen world) is whole. From the whole, the whole comes forth. When the whole is taken from the whole, the whole alone remains. Om, peace, peace, peace.

The Brahman is infinite, so the world that comes from it takes nothing away from it. Peace is said three times, for freedom from the troubles that come from oneself, from other beings and from the powers of nature (ādhyātmika, ādhibhautika, ādhidaivika).
m01: All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is to be covered by the Lord (seen as dwelt in by Him). Enjoy by renouncing it; do not covet anyone's wealth. ॥1॥

Śaṅkara reads tyaktena as “by renunciation”: one who sees the Lord as the Self of all should give up all desires. Kasya svid dhanam can also mean “for whose is wealth?”, i.e. wealth belongs to no one. Many read the second line as “enjoy what He has given”.
m02: Doing works (karma) here, one may wish to live a hundred years. For you, living so as a human being, there is no way other than this by which work does not cling to a person. ॥2॥
Śaṅkara takes mantra 1 as the path of knowledge for those who can renounce, and this mantra as the path of works, such as the agnihotra, for those who cannot yet do so.
m03: Those worlds are called “demonic”, covered in blind darkness. Whoever kills the Self goes to them after leaving the body. ॥3॥
“Killers of the Self” are those who, in ignorance, lose sight of the ever-present Self (Śaṅkara). Asuryāḥ may also be read as “sunless”.
m04: The Self is unmoving and one, yet swifter than the mind. The senses (devas) never reached it, for it was always ahead. Standing still, it outruns all that run. Because it is, Mātariśvā (the life-breath of the cosmos) sustains the workings of all beings. ॥4॥
Unmoving in itself, the Self only seems to move because it is reflected in the moving mind and senses (Śaṅkara).
m05: It moves, and it does not move. It is far, and it is near. It is within all this, and it is outside all this. ॥5॥
Far for the ignorant, who cannot reach it in ages; near for the wise, to whom it is their own Self (Śaṅkara).
m06: One who sees all beings in the Self alone, and the Self in all beings, no longer shrinks from anything. ॥6॥
m07: When, for the one who knows, all beings have become the Self itself, what delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who sees this oneness? ॥7॥
m08: He (the Self) pervades all; He is radiant, bodiless, without wound, without sinews, pure, untouched by sin. The seer, the knower of all, above all and self-existent, He has rightly assigned their duties to the eternal years (the creators). ॥8॥

Śaṅkara: “bodiless” rules out the subtle body, “without wound and sinews” the gross body, “pure” the causal body (ignorance). The “eternal years” are the Prajāpatis, the creators, each given his work.
m09: Those who worship avidyā alone enter blind darkness; into darkness greater still, as it were, go those who delight in vidyā alone. ॥9॥

Śaṅkara: avidyā is ritual work (karma) and vidyā is meditation on the deities, not the knowledge of the Self; mantras 9–11 teach that the two be practised together. Viśiṣṭādvaita (Vedānta Deśika) reads them as works and knowledge together leading to liberation; Sri Aurobindo, as knowledge of multiplicity and of unity.
m10: One result, they say, comes from vidyā, and another from avidyā. So we have heard from the wise who explained it to us. ॥10॥
Śaṅkara: by work one reaches the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka); by meditation, the world of the gods (devaloka).
m11: One who knows vidyā and avidyā both together crosses over death by avidyā and attains immortality by vidyā. ॥11॥

For Śaṅkara, “death” here is natural action and knowledge, crossed by ritual work; the “immortality” is becoming one with the deity meditated on, which is relative, not final liberation. Other schools take it as liberation itself.
m12: Those who worship asambhūti (the unmanifest) enter blind darkness; into darkness greater still, as it were, go those who delight in sambhūti (the manifest) alone. ॥12॥

Śaṅkara: asambhūti is prakṛti, the unmanifest cause; sambhūti is Hiraṇyagarbha, the manifest Brahman. Mantras 12–14 teach that the two meditations be practised together. Others read the pair as becoming and non-becoming, or as the Absolute and the world.
m13: One result, they say, comes from sambhava (the manifest), and another from asambhava (the unmanifest). So we have heard from the wise who explained it to us. ॥13॥
Śaṅkara: from worship of Hiraṇyagarbha come powers such as aṇimā (becoming subtle at will); from worship of prakṛti, absorption into it (prakṛtilaya).
m14: One who knows sambhūti and vināśa (the perishable) both together crosses over death through vināśa and attains immortality through sambhūti. ॥14॥

Śaṅkara reads vināśa, “that which perishes”, as the manifest Hiraṇyagarbha, and sambhūti here as asambhūti, the unmanifest (the a lost in sandhi); the immortality is absorption into prakṛti. Others read it as it stands: the imperishable and the perishable known together.
m15: The face of Truth is covered by a golden vessel. O Pūṣan (the Sun, nourisher of all), uncover it, so that I, devoted to the Truth, may see it. ॥15॥
The prayer of a seeker at life's end, asking to reach the Truth, the Person in the sun's disc (Śaṅkara). Mantras 15–18 also close the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (5.15).
m16: O Pūṣan, lone seer, Yama (controller of all), Sūrya, son of Prajāpati, spread apart your rays, gather in your light. Your most blessed form I see. That Person yonder — He am I. ॥16॥
“He am I”: the seeker does not ask as a servant, for the Person in the sun is his own Self (Śaṅkara).
m17: Let my breath go to the immortal all-pervading Air; then let this body end in ashes. Om! O mind, remember, remember what has been done; O mind, remember, remember what has been done. ॥17॥
A prayer at the time of death. Kratu is the mind, which wills; Om addresses Brahman as Agni (Śaṅkara). The repetition shows earnestness.
m18: O Agni, O god who knows all our deeds, lead us by the good path to wealth (the fruit of our deeds). Keep from us the crooked sin. We offer you salutations again and again in words. ॥18॥
The good path is the northern path (devayāna), free of return, unlike the southern path of birth and death (Śaṅkara). This mantra is also Ṛgveda 1.189.1.
